newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe stocks seen bullish on rate cut hopes.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe stocks seen bullish on rate cut hopes.

text.p: Zimbabwe's booming stock market is likely to continue rising in coming months on expectations of cuts in interest rates following a dramatic fall in annual inflation, market officials and analysts said on Wednesday.
The bourse was already soaring as it relished a dip in money market rates over the last six months and a string of good company results.

Buyers were also encouraged by a recent central Reserve Bank decision allowing foreign investors to buy up to 40 percent of total shareholding in a listed company, up from the the previous 35 percent ceiling.

The Zimbabwe Stock Exchange's key industrial index has soared 80.7 percent over the past nine months, breaching this week -- for the first time ever -- the 7,000 pyschological barrier. It closed Tuesday's trading session at 7,176.55.

"It has gone up at a phenomenal pace and over the next few months it should continue bullish as the possiblity of banks cutting their lending rates further is now quite strong with the fall in inflation," said Savvas Kyriakides, managing director of share market and economic analysts Dataworld.

Zimbabwe's commercial banks last month cut their lending rates by two percentage points to 30 percent after inflation slowed to 22 percent in July from a high of 28 percent in January and as interest rates on the local money market fell.

On Monday, hopes of further cuts were bolstered by the publication of latest annual inflation data which indicated year-on-year consumer price index (CPI) at a three-year low of 17.7 percent in August, surprising many economic analysts, some of whom were expecting it to rise on a spate of price hikes.
"The fall in inflation in August was greater than anybody anticipated. It is amazing," Kyriakides told Reuters.

Economic analysts, including Eric Bloch, attributed the figure to lower food prices -- which they said had a significant weighting on the CPI basket -- this year on the back of a bumper harvest in agriculture-led Zimbabwe.
"They (food prices) are substantially lower now -- between 35 and 40 percent -- from last year and that's the single biggest factor behind the fall in inflation in August," Bloch said.

On Wednesday, Zimbabwe Stock Exchange (ZSE) chief executive Anthony Barfoot said the lower annual inflation figures boosted the potential for further lending rate cuts which would have a positive impact on industry.
Although he, Kyriakides and some brokers said the market was bound to slow its hectic pace at some point, this was bound to be just a temporary breather.
"Investors are also concerned now at lower money market rates and they are moving out of there into stocks...So the stock market is going to be very high," Barfoot said.
